title: Adipose MTP and FIT2 in the regulation of plasma lipids, obesity and atherosclerosis
text: ABSTRACT – PROJECT 1: High blood levels of apoB-containing lipoproteins (apoB-Lps) are risk factors for cardiovascular diseases. ApoB-Lp production requires microsomal triglyceride (TG) transfer protein (MTP). However, MTP’s role in adipose tissue, which does not produce apoB-Lps, is unknown. Fat storage-inducing transmembrane protein 2 (FIT2) is another TG-binding protein that is involved in lipid droplet (LD) formation in adipose tissue. While MTP functions in lumen of the endoplasmic reticulum (ER), FIT2 assists in the budding of LDs from the ER membrane towards cytosol. We hypothesize that these two TG binding proteins perform different functions that affect adipocyte biology, hepatic lipid metabolism, and atherosclerosis. We showed that adipose-specific MTP deficient (A-Mttp−/−) mice are resistant to diet- induced obesity, hepatosteatosis and atherosclerosis, but adipose FIT2 deficiency causes hepatosteatosis and inflammation. These contrasting phenotypes compel us to ask if MTP deficiency can ameliorate pathologies associated with FIT2 deficiency. Aim 1.1: Role of adipose MTP in hypertriglyceridemia, hepatosteatosis, and atherosclerosis. We showed that adipose MTP inhibits adipose TG lipase (ATGL). We will: 1) ask if adipose MTP also modulates other lipases beyond ATGL; 2) work with P2 and P3 to elucidate mechanisms for hypertriglyceridemia and reduced hepatosteatosis; and 3) collaborate with C1–C3 to explain why atherosclerosis is lower in A-Mttp−/− mice. These studies will uncover how MTP promotes adipose TG storage and obesity. We propose that inhibiting adipose-specific MTP function will reduce obesity and atherosclerosis. Aim 1.2: Role of MTP and FIT2 in adipose biology, hepatosteatosis, and atherosclerosis. Given the distinct roles and sites of action of MTP and FIT2 within adipocytes, we will study the effect of adipose-specific MTP and FIT2 deficiencies on whole-body metabolism, adipose lipolysis, and atherosclerosis, and ask if MTP deficiency ameliorates FIT2-associated pathology with help from C1–C3 and expertise from P2 and P3. Our studies will: 1) provide novel information on the roles of adipose MTP and FIT2 in adipose, liver, and vascular biology; 2) generate novel mouse models; 3) explain roles of MTP and FIT2 in metabolism, TG hydrolysis, and FA secretion and oxidation; and 4) define how adipose–liver crosstalk controls obesity, hypertriglyceridemia, hepatosteatosis, and atherosclerosis. Elucidating the mechanisms of apoB-Lps production depends on collaboration with P2. We will then work with P3 to: 1) study intravascular catabolism of apoB-Lps produced by adipose–specific MTP- and FIT2-deficient mice, 2) monitor apoB-Lp uptake by endothelial cells, and 3) elucidate pro- or anti-inflammatory responses in adipocytes and macrophages. Bioinformatics analyses of RNA-seq and single cell RNA-seq (by C1), Lp characterization (by C2), and atherosclerosis studies (by C3) will yield novel insights into how adipose-specific proteins regulate metabolism.

title: Leveraging Mammalian Cancers, Platinum-Quality Genome Assemblies, and Large-Scale Data to Identify Mechanisms of Rare Human Cancers
text:
The emerging field of comparative oncology may provide a novel solution to rare human cancer studies, as
genomic resources, reference genomes and non-human model cancer sequencing data are proliferating rapidly.
We propose to, for the first time, develop and apply new machine learning methods to jointly analyze and
integrate information from hundreds of mammalian genomes to identify pan-mammalian mechanisms of cancer
resistance and susceptibility, and apply those insights in human cancers. To disseminate this date to the wider
community and catalyze further research we will develop a tumor compendium, portal, and toolkit that will allow
other researchers to leverage pan-mammalian comparative genomics.

title: Mapping the Cellular Responses to DNA Double-Strand Breaks Using On-Demand CRISPR technologies and High-resolution Fluorescence Microscopy
text:
Maintaining genome integrity is an essential task of all cells, and imperfect repair
of the damaged genome is responsible for a myriad of human diseases, ranging
from aggressive cancers to defective immune systems. This research proposal
aims to incorporate on-demand CRISPR technologies and quantitative biophysical
approaches to investigate the complex DNA damage responses induced by DNA
double-strand breaks (DSBs) in living mammalian cells. Revealing the detailed
spatiotemporal information of DDR will inform how kinetics, structures, and
chromatin status modulate DSB repair pathway choices, transcription activity, and
their interplay with the innate immune systems, providing valuable information
complementary to traditional steady-state biochemical and genetic approaches.

title: Global Initiative for Neuropsychiatric Genetics Research in Education
text:
The last decade has seen meaningful investment not just in establishing large population genetics studies
but also in training computational scientists to analyze the data. Utilizing this data to uncover the biological
mechanisms of chronic diseases, such as mental health disorders, requires well-trained multidisciplinary
research teams who can speak the language of genetics, whether they are contributing from a clinical or
computational perspective, and Uganda represents a critical setting given its high mental health burden,
rapidly expanding genomic resources, and central role in large NIMH-funded psychiatric genetics cohorts.
Therefore, we aim to train a cadre of both clinical and computational scientists at Makerere University,
learning together the skills needed to lead research in mental health genetics, in order to generate
contextually grounded discoveries that enhance the relevance, generalizability, and translational impact of
psychiatric genomics for patients both globally and specifically in the US.

title: Training to Prevent Anal Cancer (TPAC)
text: Anal cancer incidence and mortality are rising in the United States, especially among individuals with specific immunosuppressive conditions or histories of HPV-associated disease. This proposal will develop and evaluate a scalable, evidence-based training program to equip clinical providers with the knowledge and skills necessary to detect and manage precancerous anal lesions, ultimately improving early detection and reducing anal cancer burden.

title: The Biological Salience of Dimensions of Early Life Stress in Predicting Psychopathology
text:
This project aims to identify how early life stress becomes biologically embedded to increase risk for
adolescent psychopathology by examining stress-responsive biological systems and the genetic and
environmental factors that shape them. By identifying how these biological mechanisms, including
physiological indicators of neuroendocrine, immune, and epigenetic functioning, mediate risk for mental health
problems, this research will inform the development of personalized, biologically informed prevention strategies
to reduce the public health burden of youth psychological outcomes.

title: Developing a Novel Causal Discovery Framework to Unveil Individualized Cell-Cell Communication Networks
text:
Differences in the cell composition and functional states of cells within individual tissue environments lead to
tissue environment heterogeneity. The proposed project aims to develop a computational framework
integrating deep learning and causal discovery algorithms to unveil the individualized (or instance-specific) cell-
cell communication networks (CCCNs) underlying tissue environment heterogeneity of individual tissue
samples. The versatility of this framework enables its application to study CCCNs among cells in both normal
physiological conditions and various disease microenvironments, which enhances the understanding of
heterogeneity and promotes the development of precision medicine.

title: Effects of Polymeric Mucin Expression on Lung Carcinogenesis
text:
The overall goal of the proposed research is to understand the factors that contribute to the development and
progression of lung adenocarcinoma, a form of cancer that accounts for 40% of lung cancer cases,
disproportionately affects veterans, increases with age, and is associated with tobacco smoke and
deployment-related exposures. Given these demographics, armed services members and veterans represent
an at-risk population for lung adenocarcinoma. Therefore, veterans and their families will benefit significantly
from our improved understanding of lung adenocarcinoma progression and the development of new treatment
strategies for a disease that presently has only a 20% five-year survival rate.

title: Novel Cell Culture Supplement from Adipocyte-Origin Megakaryocytes and Platelets
text:
In cell culture, growth supplements provide essential nutrients, growth factors, and hormones critical for
maintaining cell health and promoting proliferation, making them indispensable in biotechnology and medicine.
However, widely used supplements such as FBS and hPL have significant drawbacks, including concerns
related to safety, standardization, cost, scalability, and ethical considerations. To address these issues, we
recently tested the hypothesis that hPL-like supplement could be produced from dedifferentiated fat (DFAT)
cells derived mature megakaryocytes (MKs) and platelets. Preliminary data indicated that the lysate from the
mixture of these cells, referred to as human mature MKs and platelets lysate (hMPL), promoted mesenchymal
stem cell (MSC) proliferation. The goal of this proposal is to demonstrate that hMPL is a competitive alternative
to existing growth supplements, such as FBS and hPL, by evaluating its mitogenic activity across various stem
cell types, ease of production, safety, standardization, cost-effectiveness, scalability, and reproducibility.

title: Understanding dynamics and phenotypic consequences of clonal hematopoiesis caused by mosaic chromosomal alterations
text:
As individuals age, mutations can occur in the DNA of their blood-forming stem cells, leading to the
proliferation of a clone of cells with the same mutation. Occurring in over 10% of people over 60 years old,
these mutations can affect large regions of chromosomes and are associated with increased risks of cancer,
infections, heart disease, and overall mortality. This study will analyze data from > 1 million individuals to
identify what influences the rate of this clonal expansion and to determine the diseases associated with higher
expansion rates.

title: Rac guanine nucleotide exchange factors in lung cancer
text: Our studies identified specific Guanine nucleotide Exchange Factors (GEFs) for the small G-protein Rac1 expressed in human lung adenocarcinoma cells that were required for their motility and invasive activities. The goal is to elucidate the involvement of these Rac-GEFs in disease progression. We will generate animal models to determine their roles in metastasis and examine at a mechanistic level their relationship with oncogenic KRAS and EGFR.

title: Functions of PRDM paralogs in craniofacial cartilage development
text:
The cranial neural crest-derived chondrocytes making up the cartilaginous structures of the craniofacial skeleton
must undergo a highly dynamic process of condensation, positional orientation, intercalation, growth,
differentiation, and maturation before establishing a cartilaginous template that will serve as a scaffold for
subsequent bone formation. Alterations to these highly orchestrated processes are associated with birth defects
and craniofacial abnormalities including cleft lip with or without cleft palate and micrognathia. This proposed
research will examine the specific importance of two chromatin modifiers, the histone methyltransferases,
PRDM3 and PRDM16, during chondrocyte development in the formation of the craniofacial skeleton.

title: Targeting Alternative Lengthening of Telomeres in Cancer
text:
While normal cells have limited lifespans, cancer cells overcome this limitation through key adaptions we
do not fully understand, enabling unlimited cell division and leading into continued tumor growth. Using
different innovative approaches, this project aims to understand the mechanisms underlying how cancer
cells overcome this limitation on lifespan and develop approaches to target the key factors enabling this,
holding promise to improve outcomes for patients with brain, soft tissue, and other malignancies.

title: Elucidating microvascular contributions to cognitive impairment at single-cell resolution
text:
Cerebral small vessel disease (CSVD) is a leading cause of dementia and stroke, but understanding its
underlying molecular and cellular mechanisms remains challenging. Recent single-nucleus sequencing studies
have provided powerful insights into various neurological diseases; but because current techniques do not
efficiently capture human brain vessels, our understanding of CSVD has lagged behind. To bridge this gap, we
will isolate human brain vascular nuclei from 191 curated CSVD brain samples with our new VINE-seq method
and apply the latest multimodal single-nucleus technologies to elucidate the molecular and cellular processes
that contribute to early-, mid-, and late-stage CSVD.

title: B Cell Specificity and Repertoire Across Tissues and Age
text: Immune responses need to occur in diverse anatomical sites to provide protective immunity to pathogens with different infection and tissue tropism characteristics throughout the human lifespan. B cells and plasma cells responsible for humoral immunity show differences in phenotypic subsets in primary and secondary lymphoid tissues, mucosal sites, and other diverse sites in both mice and humans. In contrast to well-studied tissue resident T-cells, much less is known about the phenotypes, pathogen specificities, and tissue adaptations of tissue-resident memory B-cells (BRM) in lymphoid organs including lymph nodes associated with different mucosal sites. Our preliminary data show that memory B cell (MBC) subsets differ in their proportions in different human tissues and vary according to their antigen specificity, with increased proportions of non-class switched memory for long-lasting childhood vaccines for tetanus and measles, and increased atypical phenotype memory for SARS-CoV-2 spike and influenza antigens. Aging is associated with greater proportions of SARS-CoV-2 and influenza MBC with the atypical phenotype, and with age-related changes in tissue residency and turnover. Our central hypotheses are therefore that antigen-specific B cell populations 1. differ systematically in phenotype and class-switching between human lymphoid tissues, 2. have distinct antigen-specific B cell receptor repertoires, and 3. show dynamic subset-specific changes over age. Project 2 will conduct an in-depth analysis across donors, age groups and tissues of B cell antigen binding specificity, B cell receptor sequences, and cellular phenotype, and will define secreted antibody repertoire specificity for a broad range of human pathogen and vaccine antigens. We will use innovative single-cell, serological and imaging techniques to map the clonal and BCR basis of tissue-associated humoral immunity. We have validated a highly multiplexed DNA-tagged antigen panel for antigen-specific B cell sorting and transcriptome, BCR and antigen tag sequencing, combined with deep bulk B cell receptor heavy chain sequencing and monoclonal antibody (mAb) characterization. In parallel, we will differentiate memory B cells from each tissue to antibody-secreting cells and test supernatant Ab binding to very large pathogen antigen libraries, to further define tissue-enriched B cell memory repertoires. We will test mAbs from single cells to define their functional activities. These high-resolution B cell data will be integrated with spatial transcriptomic analysis of B cell subsets and their niche localization with age. Close coordination and data analyses with Projects 1, 3, and the Single Cell and Systems Immunology Core C will provide broader immunological context to maximize the impact of these tissue B cell and antibody studies.

title: Natural Language Screening to Improve Early Recognition of Child Physical Abuse in Emergency Care Settings
text:
This project will improve the early recognition of physical abuse in infants, to improve the chance that they
can be protected from ongoing violence, permanent injury, and death. Despite decades of education,
awareness-building, screening by nurses, and other efforts, abuse is often missed in the youngest children
who cannot speak for themselves. This project will test a program of automated screening by computers that
can analyze data from the medical chart in real-time to alert healthcare providers to findings that should raise
concern for abuse, but which are often missed.

title: Translational Science Laboratory Shared Resource
text: The Hollings Cancer Center (HCC) Translational Science Laboratory (TSL), a new shared resource as of 2017, works closely with clinical, translational, and basic scientists to drive the development and use of novel biomarker assays to provide the most innovative discovery, pre-clinical and correlative science studies. The mission of TSL is to facilitate the translation of basic science research to the clinical setting and vice versa to improve diagnosis and treatment strategies for cancer patients. Moreover, TSL provides expertise in drug development and helps basic and translational scientists explore pre-clinical hypotheses and conceive and execute strategic, correlative science plans for clinical trials at HCC. Specifically, TSL aims to: 1) provide high-quality molecular services, providing timely NGS-based library preparation dependably and cost-effectively; 2) perform consulting on high-dimensional transcriptomic and protein profiling analyses, the design and execution of single-cell/nuclei sequencing, bulk NGS, NanoString nCounter analysis, spatial transcript/protein profiling experiments, and quantitative multiplex immunofluorescence; and 3) offer method development, training, and education. Directed by Jian Ouang, PhD (CBI), and staffed by four technical experts, this facility provides extensive molecular genomics/transcriptomics and histology/IHC/multiplex immunofluorescence capabilities, an active educational platform, and the development of new methodologies, plus assists in data analysis and interpretation for publication. Services offered through TSL include: consultation, training, education, data analyses, preparation of data for publication, and a full suite of molecular services, including automated nucleic acid (RNA, DNA, miRNA) extraction from various sources (whole blood, tissue, cells, FFPE tissue), nucleic acid quantification and QC, DNA shearing, droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), next-generation sequencing library preparation (bulk RNAseq, ChIPseq, whole genome methylation-seq, ATACseq, miRNAseq, targeted capture), single-cell/single-nuclei RNAseq and Multiome (single-nuclei RNAseq+ATACseq), NanoString bulk targeted transcriptomic analysis and GeoMx digital spatial profiling of both protein and RNA. The ability to provide high-dimensional RNA and protein analysis at the single-cell level has proven to be a powerful discovery tool. Forty-seven (47) HCC members used TSL during the current cycle, providing key data contributing to four successful NCI-funded grant applications and 16 peer-reviewed publications in high-impact journals, including Sci Immunol, Cell Reports, Cell Reports Med, Cell Death and Differ and Nat Commun. In summary, the TSL Shared Resource advances, supports, and provides critical emerging molecular and spatial research tools and methodologies to the HCC community.

title: Targeting the Patient Microbiome for the Prevention of Surgical Site Infection in Spine Surgery
text:
Surgical site infection (SSI) is a major public health problem with devastating perioperative outcomes, affecting
as many as 1 in 20 patients undergoing instrumented spine surgery. The development of more effective
strategies for SSI prevention in spine surgery is significantly limited by a lack of fundamental understanding
about the origins of causative bacteria, the basic pathogenesis of spinal wound infection, the microbiome of the
back, and the role of antimicrobial resistance to surgical prophylaxis. The proposed research will use bacterial
genomic methods to define these key mechanisms, including the roles of the patient microbiome, sex, and
anatomy, and will be used to develop new, scientifically informed strategies for SSI prevention in spine
surgery.

title: Core J: Virology and Molecular Biomarkers
text: The Virology and Molecular Biomarkers (VMB) Core (Core J) provides state-of-the-art resources to catalyze basic, translational, clinical, and behavioral HIV/SIV research in support of Emory CFAR’s mission. The Core comprises three highly collaborative units with complementary resources and expertise. The Translational Virology Unit (TVU), develops and implements viral quantitative assays supporting primarily nonhuman primate (NHP) models of AIDS pathogenesis, prevention, therapy, and cure research. The CLIA/CAP-certified Clinical Virology Unit (CVU), provides virologic and molecular diagnostic assays for clinical, translational, and behavioral studies of HIV infection, sexually transmitted infections (STI), co-infections, and related syndromes. The Viral Reservoirs Unit (VRU) develops and implements assays that quantify the viral reservoir on antiretroviral therapy (ART) to support cure research. The VMB Core provides innovative, standardized, high throughput viral quantitative assays, nimbly adapts to the needs of HIV/SIV researchers in an ever-evolving field, and serves as a resource for training early-stage investigators in molecular virologic assays. The Core effectively responds to the needs of an evolving field through the development, validation, and provision of: 1) standardized plasma viral load assays for HIV, SIV, and SHIV; 2) cell-associated DNA and RNA assays for SIV and HIV; 3) molecular diagnostic assays for HIV-associated co-infections (HBV, HCV, CMV) and STIs; 4) HIV/SIV quantitative assays in non-standard specimens; and 5) molecular assays to measure the viral reservoir under ART. The Core expanded its services with the addition of the VRU to support HIV cure research, including the establishment, maintenance, and eradication of the persistent reservoir of latently infected cells under ART. In the next project period, the VMB Core will further the range and overall performance of provided assays and services and leverage the Illumina MiSeq deep sequencing platform to characterize virus integration sites, viral evolution in response to new therapies, and the relationship of the genital/gut microbiomes with HIV transmission/pathogenesis. The Core will continue training activities in molecular virological techniques and gene assays, providing expert consultation, and expanding opportunities for stakeholder engagement through these specific aims: Aim 1. Expand the capacity of the Translational Virology Unit to provide a greater range of assays to support studies of pathogenesis, prevention, and therapy of SIV/SHIV in NHPs. Aim 2. Provide established and novel assays required for HIV human subjects research and clinical trials through customized clinical testing in the CLIA-certified Clinical Virology Unit. Aim 3. Support the growth in cure studies in NHPs through established and novel assays measuring the virus reservoir in ART-suppressed, SIV/SHIV-infected NHP in the Viral Reservoirs Unit.

title: Scientific Core: CRISPRi mouse husbandry and AAV delivery
text: CRISPR Mouse Husbandry and AAV Delivery (Mouse Core) The overarching goal of this Scientific Core is to support in vivo Perturb-seq experiments to map gene programs in a consistent, coordinated fashion across all three Projects by providing standardized mouse models and adeno-associated virus (AAV) guide RNA (gRNA) libraries. All three Projects will use the same Cre-inducible dCas9-KRAB (CRISPRi) mouse line with the same gRNA library packaged into AAVs for in vivo Perturb-seq. To investigate candidate causal gene function in an appropriate vascular disease model, each Project will require breeding the CRISPRi allele with other disease-specific alleles and lineage-tracing marker alleles. Mouse alleles employed in these studies are being sourced from multiple laboratories in different backgrounds. Thus, it is critical that the individual mouse lines be validated, and their authenticity be managed in accordance with strict lineage control through genotyping all alleles and maintaining comprehensive breeding records. Centralized mouse model generation in a homogenous relevant background is key to comparing Perturb-seq data for the same genes across different cell types and organ systems, and to mapping gene programs in a consistent, coordinated fashion across all 3 Projects. To this end, we are proposing four Specific Aims: 1) to establish mouse colonies that will provide Cre-inducible vascular cell-specific conditional knockout and lineage tracing for the in vivo studies to validate coronary artery disease (CAD) and pulmonary arterial hypertension (PAH) genes in vascular disease models; 2) to combine the Cre-inducible dCas9-KRAB (CRISPRi) allele with CAD and PAH animal disease models; 3) to generate high quality AAVs with pooled gRNA libraries that efficiently transduce endothelial cells (ECs) in the aorta, brain, and lung; and 4) to optimize and improve technologies required for in vivo Perturb-seq. Through these activities, the Mouse Core will provide breeder mice of the needed genotype for expansion to each Project with breeding and genotyping instructions. The Core will also provide high-titer, high-purity AAVs containing gRNA libraries for in vivo Perturb-seq along with dosing information. Working closely with personnel from each of the 3 Projects, the Mouse Core will help improve the efficiency of in vivo Perturb-seq throughout the 5-year program. This Core will be administered by Thomas Quertermous (Overall PI and Core PI), Chong Park (Overall Project Manager, and Co-I on this Core), and seasoned senior research assistant Ramendra Kundu. Drs. Quertermous and Kundu have worked together for two decades generating and phenotyping genetically modified mouse models, and Dr. Park was previously the Project Manager for the Keck miRNA Knockout Mouse Project and Director of the Embryonic Stem Cell Targeting Core at UCSF. The Mouse Core will bring together an unparalleled set of technologies in the cardiovascular field to study two of the leading causes of human disability and death, and support collaborations on understanding shared genetics between these diseases and common cell types.
